items.title: Importance and Methods of Gene Regulation

source_refs.note: The importance and methods of regulation (PDF 141-142); Figures 19.21 and 19.22 are replaced by original diagrams.

blocks.text: Regulation lets cells respond to environmental conditions and make proteins when they are needed. In multicellular organisms it is the basis of cell differentiation and morphogenesis, creating different cell types that share one genome but express different genes.

Regulation happens at several levels: the rate of transcription, the modification of mRNA after transcription, the rate of translation, and the modification of the protein after translation (its folding, stability and so on).

items: Negative regulation: regulatory proteins called repressors bind pieces of DNA called operators near the promoter and block RNA polymerase, stopping or reducing transcription.
Positive regulation: regulatory proteins called activators (or inducers) bind to the operators and start transcription or speed it up by helping RNA polymerase bind the promoter.

blocks.alt: Two DNA strips, each with a promoter, a regulatory site and a gene. Top, negative regulation: a red repressor sits on the operator and RNA polymerase cannot pass, so transcription stops or slows. Bottom, positive regulation: a green activator sits beside RNA polymerase on the promoter and a long arrow shows transcription starting or speeding up.
blocks.caption: Negative and positive regulation (original diagram after Figure 19.21).
blocks.long_description: Genes carry regulatory sequences to which regulatory proteins bind. In negative regulation a repressor binds an operator near the promoter and blocks RNA polymerase, stopping or reducing transcription. In positive regulation an activator binds a regulatory site and helps RNA polymerase bind the promoter, starting transcription or increasing its rate.

blocks.text: In eukaryotes genes can also be switched on or off during splicing of the mRNA. Specific regulatory proteins in specific cell types remove the pieces of mRNA, introns or exons, in different ways, so mRNAs of different lengths are made and more than one polypeptide can come from a single gene.

blocks.alt: One pre-mRNA with exons 1, 2, 3 and 4 separated by grey intron lines. Arrows lead to two cell types: in A the mRNA keeps exons 1, 2 and 4, in B exons 1, 3 and 4, and each makes a different protein shown as three coloured beads.
blocks.caption: Alternative splicing (original diagram after Figure 19.22).
blocks.long_description: In eukaryotes genes can also be regulated during splicing. Specific regulatory proteins in specific cell types control which pieces of the pre-mRNA are removed, introns or even exons, so mRNAs of different lengths are made from one gene and more than one polypeptide can be produced from it.
